email.scenario: Last weekend you took the self-guided outdoor tour at Willowbrook Art Garden. The printed stop map you were handed at the entrance numbered each sculpture differently from the numbered signs posted at the actual stops, and by the third stop you and other visitors were unsure which artwork matched which map entry.
email.subject: Mismatched Stop Numbers on the Garden Tour Map
bullets: Describe how the printed stop map's numbers did not match the posted signs at each stop.
Explain at what point during the tour you and other visitors became confused.
Request a corrected map before the next scheduled tour.

academicDiscussion.professorPost: Many streaming platforms now sign new users up for an algorithm-curated "discovery playlist" instead of a blank personal library that a listener would build track by track. This changes the first experience a new user has with the platform, and it also determines what data the algorithm has to work with. Do you think platforms should default new users into curated playlists, or should new users start with an empty library and build it themselves? Why?

studentPosts.name: Maya
studentPosts.post: I think curated playlists are the better default. Most new users don't know what to search for on an unfamiliar platform, and a blank library feels like extra work before you've even decided if you like the service. A ready-made playlist gets people listening immediately, and they can adjust it later.

studentPosts.name: Tomas
studentPosts.post: I disagree with Maya. If the algorithm curates your very first listening sessions, it starts shaping your taste before you've had any chance to explore on your own, and those early plays become the data it leans on afterward. A blank library takes more effort at first, but it keeps your early recommendations tied to choices you actually made.
